item.content:encoded:
This one was interesting but I think it could do with a rewrite to bring it up to current standards. I know a lot of the things I've covered here were mentioned in other comments but I wrote the majority of it before reading all the other comments.

Potential issues I noted:

+ show block
– hide block
  • Use of the term 'rage state': there's a bit in A Few Examples of Things Not To Do In An SCP And What To Do Instead that explains the issues with the term much better than I can.
  • "…in a room six (6) metres in length and six (6) metres in width.": Since the room's dimensions are describing a three dimensional space, this line should include a height. Also 6mx6m seems like a lot of space for a SCP that, at most, is a loose collection of body parts from a couple of cadavers.
  • "…and a new cadaver wheeled in…": "wheeled in" doesn't fit the clinical tone of the rest of the article. A potential replacement could be "and a new cadaver provided"
  • "When without a body, SCP-797 will attempt to escape its containment.": I took "body" to mean when not provided with a cadaver, but on second thought it could mean when it lacks SCP-797-01 as evidenced by the later line "When surrounded by SCP-797-01, SCP-797 shows no desire to escape". The line could be modified to something like "When SCP-797-01 ceases to exist through decomposition or damage, SCP-797 will search for new parts to harvest. If no suitable body parts are readily available, SCP-797 will attempt to breach containment in order to locate material to recreate SCP-797-01."
  • "…a human cadaver of any age, condition, gender, or race is to be deposited in SCP-797's containment.": The article mentions that parts must eventually be replaced due to natural rot. Therefore, it might be advisable to provide cadavers of a certain quality (recently deceased, lacking notable decomposition, or in other words "fresh") to ensure that SCP-797-01 won't fall apart prematurely causing SCP-797 to breach containment. This would have the extra effect of lowering the body "cost" of maintaining containment, as not needing to replace parts of -01 as often would mean replacing cadavers less often. On the same vein, maybe a part about keeping containment as cold as SCP-797 will tolerate in order to slow decomposition would help.
  • "Rarely, the subject will attempt to use SCP-797-01 to talk, producing a [REDACTED] sound…": I know that many commenters have mentioned this one but that [REDACTED] seems out of place.
  • "… including thirty (30) centimeters of an elderly woman…": Despite the sensible chuckle I had at this sentence, it doesn't really fit the article. There's been no mention up to this point of SCP-797 being able to harvest parts from living bodies. Also, the sentence is written as if the woman is still alive ("suffering from pancreatic cancer"), even though I'm pretty sure that if you straight up remove 30 centimeters of any part of a human body suddenly, it would be fatal. If it would be something potentially less than lethal (e.g. 30 centimeters of skin), that detail should be included.
  • "…three (3) kidneys (ringed seal, human, donor organ)…": The breakdown of kidney sources is a bit superfluous, as "donor organ" would just be another human kidney.
  • "…from a thirteen (13) year old male, dying of [REDACTED].": This redaction also seems unnecessary. The patient is already unidentified, and honestly what he is dying of is not important enough to the article for the reader to wonder what it is.
  • The addendum, as a whole, is hard to read and doesn't seem like an appropriate tone or diction for a doctor working in such a clinical setting.

As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

Anyway, gotta put the -1 on it for now but I would love to see this article again after some TLC.

The concept of this piece is really cool, as is the idea of it, but there are some things that stand out as in need of possible revision.

1. Rage state. Maybe it would be less of an issue if you didn't use those exact words.
2. Tonal issues throughout, and a couple of missing words. (30 cm of an elderly woman? Which 30 cm? 30 cm of what?)
3. Some kinda weird redaction regarding this thing's vocalizations and the diseases the patients of its first victims are suffering from.

I'm no-voting this. I realize it's old, but it's a solid concept, and wouldn't take much work to make it really shine.

item.content:encoded:
1. Well it results in the body rotting to a pulp, a heck of a lot of bacteria around, and SCP-797 doing whatever it can to escape. I assumed the reader would put the fact I mentioned 'bacteria', 'when away from SCP-797 will use whatever it can to escape' together.

2. Duly noted, I thought I edited that out. My bad. As for the sound, I already addressed that with that I didn't know what would be most appropriate, since each person apparently perceived it differently, so even if it is obvious to you, it is obvious to me, and it is obvious to Smascher, we still imagine completely different things. Because of this, I at first wrote a list of noises it would produce, but felt that my imagination alone was not good enough and someone might say 'well why not this?', resulting a long and overly comprehensible list.

3. It's very much applied that it is sentient, as it tries to talk and communicate and is easily frustrated. The use of 'subject' was very much purposeful there. I also halfway didn't know what I was to replace it /with/, since SCP-797 all over the place just was ugly and terrible writing.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm coming into this kind of late, so the article I'm seeing is pretty well polished, with many recommendations already implemented.
The idea is original (not easy to do) AND you managed to create clear underlying motivations for its behavior (intent to interact, rage at failure to do so) which is excellent.

My issues:

1. I am a lazy Foundation researcher. Honestly, I'd rather not take the trouble of putting a class-D corpse in there. What happens if I don't? (Failure to do so results in [REDACTED] and should be avoided if at all possible)?

2. As Smascher said, there's no real reason to cut out an adjective in the "throwing flesh" and "[REDACTED] sound" sentences. Cutting the adjectives out kinda makes it look like the writer was too lazy to pick a good one. I imagine "unintelligible" fitting there, but it's not a disaster to leave as-is.

3. I would avoid referring to SCP-797 as a "subject". You could use that word for sentient SCPs if you had to, humanoid ones in particular… but I think it's generally avoided, especially with animate objects like 797.

Final result:
Definite upvote, nice first SCP.

P.S.
If you want to make your second picture sit on the left, just change your code from: [[div style="float:right; margin:0 2em 1em 2em; width:300px; border:0;"]] to [[div style="float:left; margin:0 2em 1em 2em; width:300px; border:0;"]]

^ (changing "float:right; -> "float:left; obviously)
it might give it a nice aesthetic feel like SCP-165 has.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Not bad for a first go. In addition to the points made by Sorts, some minor comments:

"size of a tangerine" should be replaced with an approximate diameter in centimeters

Given the potential hazards of interaction gone awry, why are level 4 personnel permitted in the room? The Foundation tends to avoid putting more valuable personnel into dangerous situations- they're much harder to replace.

Second paragraph of Description, the last two sentences are a little disjointed. It might flow better if the high velocity of the projectiles is mentioned explicitly.

Only other things I might note are naming conventions. Procedure names are all over the map but they typically either include the SCP's number (eg procedure 797-somethingoranother) or something more ominous (eg procedure 110-Montauk or however the hell it's spelled). Amnesiacs are usually given a classification of A, B, or C. No, we have no idea what any of those mean. Mind you, there is no canon, so these are largely optional; but they do help with consistency across articles.

item.content:encoded:
Hmmm…

If you were worried about length before don't be, it was not too long.

I like the idea, but I'm not a big fan of the containment procedures and the way you've written it out. Why a female "nurse" and why a D-class one at that? The thing may be unpleasant but it isn't super deadly that we'd have to go through such a pantomime act and use disposable people to enter its chamber. And a new body every three days seems a bit much as well. I get the purpose of providing it with new parts to facilitate study and interactions with it but I think you need to reconsider the approach.
